utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what happened to these men thereafter, ultimately?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Because I went up to Sokolac privately. And when I came back in the evening -- I don't remember the details, I don't think I paid any attention because I was going about my own business. I really don't know. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said that you handed these men over to Dusko Jevic initially on the 17th of July. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- well, Dusko Jevic -- I said I handed them over to Dusko Jevic. He was there with me, so it was an operation. Dusko Jevic took those people up officially, and I'm sure that can be confirmed by him. Dule will bear me out there. That's how it was and that's what I told you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to Dusko Jevic, sir, he says he doesn't know what happened to the men and that he didn't take custody of them?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Dusko Jevic can come here into this courtroom and say that to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us, sir, how many prisoners were captured on the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 35 to 38, or rather, a total of 38, of those three children, and 35 adults, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to Dusko Jevic, there was approximately 200 men that were captured. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps Dusko captured them somewhere. As far as I remember, this is how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, he was referring to the men that were captured on the 17th of July when you were there, sir.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until noon, 12.00, by the time I arrived, what he had done before that and where he had taken them, I don't know. But when I arrived - and I'm sure Zekic can confirm that - that it's just how I said it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, didn't you see the men before you left, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can count fairly well, and had I looked in the warehouse and seen 200 people, I would have known about it. But to get 200 people in that kind of warehouse, well, it's rather a feat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the warehouse, sir, I'm talking about the 17th of July when you and Dusko Jevic and Zekic were there and captured these men.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And at that time there was a total of 38, of which three were children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those children, sir, said that there were -- there was more than 38. There were hundreds. Do you have anything to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I had to say was what I already said, and that is that I received information that there was a settling of accounts. Now, how many people were there by the school, the children can tell you that. But I know how many people surrendered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you report the soldier who you've told us about wanted to kill some of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to that soldier, when I was at the command -- well, the man died two or three days later in a looting operation, so the whole thing ended tragically, as I warned him it might.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: Did you report him to anyone?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not report him to anyone. My commander was absent. There was just me. I had -- I came to the command and told the colleagues about it, those who were there, or rather, I think Pilipovic was there, Major Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Major Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Major Pilipovic was a man who wrote lots of things. What he actually did is not clear to this day after so many years have gone by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know what he did -- he was at the command, but you don't know what he did there, or what his position was?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know what his position was. I would always see him writing something, but I didn't listen. When we had reporting, he never took part in the discussions, so I don't know what his official assignments were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you report it to the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, after Commander Blagojevic left to Zepa and further, because he was ill as far as I understood it, he had a heart ailment, he was in the operations hall all the time, nonstop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you see, I need you to focus on the question, sir. The question is: Did you report the soldier that wanted to kill the Muslims to the duty officer? It's a very simple question, and you can answer it by saying yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reported to Major Pilipovic what had happened on the ground and what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he acting as the duty officer on that day?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole time during that period, he was the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you spell his name for us, for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I can spell the surname. P-i-l-i-p-o-v-i-c. I don't know his first name to this day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you inform anyone of the capture of the men during the search of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Pilipovic in his report must have written down what I conveyed to him when I got there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is it that you conveyed to him?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I conveyed to him that 37 had been captured, or rather, 38. I beg your pardon. And of that number, three children, they were in -- with the military police, and that the others had left in the direction of Konjevic Polje with Dusko Jevic because somebody was, I suppose, supposed to send some buses to take them to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say he must have written it down because you knew him to be a very precise man. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a man who wrote the war diary of the Bratunac Brigade. I personally had an opportunity of seeing that diary when I was in Banja Luka. He showed me the diary, so I assume he would have written everything down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was his job, is to write these things down. Right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that. I don't know what his job was, but every time I saw him, he would be writing something down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And was it your obligation to inform the duty officer of the captured men?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as I arrived at the Bratunac Brigade and the operations hall, he was sitting at a table there with the duty logbook. So he, as far as I was concerned, was the duty officer. So I told him about this and automatically had discharged my duties that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say you automatically had discharged your duties, it was your duty to inform the duty officer. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right, and that's what I did. So Pilipovic, as far as I was concerned, was the duty officer at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And telling the duty officer is effectively as good as telling the commander. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right. And since I couldn't tell that to the commander, because my commander was already at Zepa at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the next day when you say you went by and saw the men that you had captured on the 17th of July at the warehouse in Konjevic Polje, can you explain why you went there.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why I went there, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there to see whether they were those people who were there, because I would probably recognise some of those people if I were to meet them, someone from that group, because I saw them personally at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ordered to go there?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I went privately. I said a moment ago I was on my way to Sokolac privately, and I would go that way frequently because I used to work there. So I was preparing for my job, and I went out of curiosity, to have a look. And I was wearing civilian clothes when I went that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And who was guarding the men?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The special police, judging by their uniforms. They were a little more elegantly dressed from the regular soldiers, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Didn't you also say to the OTP or the Office of the Prosecutor investigator - and I'm referring to page 32 in the English version, lines 9 through 12. And perhaps somebody can give you your B/C/S version, if I can ask Madam Usher for her assistance, at page 32, paragraph 1 - didn't you also say, sir, that you knew that the men who were guarding the prisoners at the warehouse were not soldiers because, and I'm quoting you at line 10, page 32: "I think they were members of some of those attached units, the units from the MUP. They were for sure not soldiers, because that was the zone of responsibility of our brigade." Isn't that how you knew?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't thinking on the basis of that, and I said very well that they weren't soldiers. And I claim now that they weren't soldiers but were members of the MUP. The special police, the civilian police, that was the MUP for me as far as I was concerned at that point in time. Now, the responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade, if we look at that part, they had already stepped out of the municipality, the border of the Bratunac municipality, because the border goes up to Konjevic Polje, that road. So you can say that that already belonged, as far as I knew, topographically speaking, to Zvornik, or Milici. I don't know. That's where the boundary is, somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not what you said, sir. You told the investigator very clearly: "Because that was the zone of responsibility of our brigade." Those are your words, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I can agree with that. I told the investigator that they weren't soldiers, that they were from the MUP, but he didn't ask me to explain whether it was the Bratunac municipality or not. I know it's the border belt; I know that for a fact myself because I lived in the area, so that's how I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And notwithstanding that he asked you to explain, sir, you said: "It was the zone of responsibility of our brigade." This is something you told him, notwithstanding that he didn't ask you. Isn't that right? It's a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, possibly I said it that way, if it says that in the translation, but I assume I went on to say -- or rather, that that's what I said. But that facility, topographically speaking, was in the Zvornik or Milici area. But that's not important. The important thing is that when I came by, those people were in that facility and we captured them -- as many as had been captured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's move on to something else then, sir. Now, on 14 July when you were on your way to Zvornik, did you happen to pass by the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I passed by on the 15th, towards the end of the 14th -- during the night between the 14th and the 15th, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you see bodies in front of the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see bodies. It was night-time, and the Bratunac/Kravica road, Oka, is on the left. There's a fence there. And I didn't know what had happened on that day had actually happened at Oka. And the investigator asked me about that, and I said I didn't see, as indeed I did not see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you not smell anything that perhaps would have caught your attention as you were passing by the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because it was night. But when I came back the next day, on the 15th that is, then along the road from Konjevic Polje to Bratunac, you could feel this in the air, smell this in the air.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you could smell it in the air on your way back is what you're saying, but not on the way there, you didn't?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on my way back from Zvornik, from Konjevic Polje towards Bratunac. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, about almost 1.000 people were killed at the Kravica warehouse, sir. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that point in time, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were driving by at night, you didn't see the loaders that were picking up the bodies and putting them in trucks and burying them in graves in Glogova. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see the trucks or the loaders on my way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that there were mass graves in Glogova, where over 1.000 bodies were buried?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I tell you here and now - and this is the truth and absolutely correct, what I'm going to tell you now - during that period I didn't deal with that at all. I wasn't interested in that, but everybody who worked and has the right to respond, be responsible, but I learnt about this later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, when -- going back to the 17th of July, you ordered the separation of the children from the rest of the men. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was -- what you were concerned with was persons born after 1980. Those are the children you wanted to -- you separated. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you made no effort to separate the elderly men? Those were not -- they were not separated. Right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that group, the average age was certainly about 40 to 45. I don't think I'm exaggerating, if I say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you see anybody that was wounded in that group?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody was wounded. Had they been wounded, they would certainly have been separated and taken to Bratunac where there was a room at the health centre where they would have been taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Would it surprise you to know, sir, that the three children you separated were, in fact, around 15 or 16 years old? Those were their ages.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of them had any documents on them. All I could do was judge by what they looked like, and the blond boy who said he was from Kasaba sort of looked older. And the ones who were nice-looking and nicely dressed, the twins, they might have been 10 or 11, but I don't really know. I wasn't interested in their age. I saw they were children; that was the important thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive orders to separate the boys?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't receive orders. I decided on my own, because I thought it would be a pity to leave those children to spend the night where the others were spending the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that the boys were used for media purposes, that they were filmed for the media?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was one of the initiators of having those children filmed by way of proof and evidence, because regardless of the fact that they had left together with Mr. Miso I was responsible for them if I had brought them there. So that's what I wanted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is the Prosecution's position, sir, that these boys were taken out, they were separated as part of an organised programme to keep the men, and to show the world that nothing was going on, that the men weren't murdered. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to another exhibit, Exhibit P501. Now, this is from the command of the Bratunac Brigade, and it's dated 17 July 1995, addressed to the Drina Corps. The name on the bottom is Vidoje Blagojevic, and it states: "Among the Muslim prisoners there are four underage children (aged between 8 and 14) who are being held in military custody in Bratunac. One of them told the commander of the unit that was searching the area about a large number of Muslim troops committing suicide or killing each other. We propose that this testimony be recorded by cameras of your press centre." Is that something that you proposed, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I proposed -- or rather, I ordered. First of all, I ordered that the military police, that the children, as I said, should be given food to eat, be given a bath, a change of clothing, and then showed them the premises where they would be. Then when I came to the operations hall, I said that those children should be medically examined, and as far as I am concerned that was proof that these children, thank heaven, are alive today and that they can come and sit down with me and say: "You, sir" -- that they won't say: "You, sir, are not telling how it was." That is why I took advantage of the occasion to be with Naser Oric on the 1st of September 2002 because I learned that they were his children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, that wasn't my question, and maybe I can be more specific. The document says one of them, one of the children, told the commander of the unit that was searching the area about a large number of Muslim troops committing suicide. And then it follows: "We propose that this testimony be used by cameras of your press centre." The question is: Did you make that proposal? You were the commander of the unit at the time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the commander of that unit. I said they should be filmed. I said that it should be said that besides the murders, atrocities, there were also mutual killings, people settling accounts among themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't say: Besides the murders and atrocities, though, does it?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was what I thought. I thought that when those children testify to what I have said yesterday and today, that when we pass through the area there were people killing each other, I'm not denying that there were also the other things. But as far as I am concerned and my operation, certainly none of the prisoners were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the children, sir, has given names of some of the men that were missing to investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I ask the relevancy, unless the next question is that in the statement that there is some indication that this gentleman was responsible for the missing of those individuals or for the killing of those individuals. I would like to know what the relevancy is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. That is the question also in our mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, I believe, Your Honour, the witness just said he doesn't know -- I think earlier he said he doesn't know what happened to the individuals, and I would like to know whether he's aware of the following information that we've received subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's been asked and answered. He said he doesn't know. That's the answer. Now, whether the children say otherwise, his answer remains the same, he doesn't know. And she's trying to bootstrap somehow to tie him in to what happened to those people later on. He indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas. We agree with you. You may move on, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've told us earlier that you were sleeping in the Bratunac town on 12 and 13th July. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were there, did you see the hundreds of men who were imprisoned on buses and in the schools?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My family house where I slept is 5 or 600 metres away from those schools, and those schools are to the east of the town centre. Therefore, I did not pass by there. And on that evening, I didn't see anything. On the following day - I can't say whether it was the 12th or the 13th - I went to the command and I saw a bus near the ceramics factory. I met two buses. And I assume those were buses used to begin the transport of civilians from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see men detained on the buses?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite truthful, I passed by in my vehicle and I didn't pay attention. I didn't look to see whether there were men, women, or children. I really didn't pay attention, because when you're driving 60 or 50 kilometres an hour, you're looking at your own lane. I saw buses, yes, but I don't know who was inside of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that about 200 men were detained in the Vuk Karadzic school and some of them were murdered on 12, 13 July there?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, no. But I did hear about it later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that over 50 men -- there were over 50 bodies of men found in and around the Vuk Karadzic school the evening of 13 and 14 July?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that they were guarded by members of the Bratunac Brigade military police and others?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who guarded them. I know it wasn't my unit. I don't know who did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the murders of 150 people in the Cerska Valley, the 16 people by the banks of the Jadar River, and the 16 people around the Sandici meadow on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, and it will be -- it will take some time, Your Honour. And also it was brought to our attention that there was a map prepared by the following witness, the witness following this witness, that was never disclosed to us. They didn't -- the Prosecution wasn't able to get it to us yesterday. So if we could have maybe a slightly additional time during this break period so I could go over that, show the map to the individual -- to the next witness, so at least he's aware of the map. So I need about 10 additional minutes with that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let's finish this witness first. Could we finish this witness in 10 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It may take a little bit longer, Your Honour, and there are other reasons why it might be a good idea to perhaps break at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm very much concerned about the time schedule. We are almost five sittings behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're on schedule, Your Honour. We're on schedule. We'll finish our witnesses for the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And this week we have six witnesses on the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, but we'll be on time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You're sure of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't want to guarantee, but I'm sure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you need a longer break?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: A longer break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: When do you suggest we resume?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if we could -- if we could resume say 25 to, 25 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 25 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Re-examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gavric.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you. I want to go back to the first document. We're going to go through several documents. These sets of documents deal with 25 May 1995. So I would like you to first look at what has been marked as P39 -- I mean, P397, I'm sorry. 397. This was a document that was shown to you earlier. Now, if we look at the second paragraph, it says here: "At 1000 hours, the transfer of duties of commander of the 1st Bratunac Brigade was carried out in the presence of the commander of the Drina Corps, Major General Zivanovic, and the president of the Bratunac Municipal Assembly, Ljubo Simic." Sir, from this paragraph here, can we conclude that this was the day when Mr. Blagojevic became the commander of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this combat report, that's what it says. And that's how it should be. On the 25th of May, whether that was the day Mr. Blagojevic assumed his duties, well it says here that it happened at 1000 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And if we go all the way down to the bottom, we can see the time, can we not, when this document was submitted to the Drina Corps command at the bottom right-hand. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And that would be 4.30 in the afternoon, which is about the time when daily reports generally go out. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I could show you now -- I'm going to walk you one by one. The next document, same day, 25 May 1995, Prosecution Exhibit 855. This was the document that had your name on it. Right? Now, if we look at the first line it says: "At 1907," so that would be what time? That's 7.00 in the evening, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This would be after the daily report had been submitted to the Drina Corps. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go down to the bottom, we see that this was submitted, though the incident occurred at 1907, this report was submitted at 2010 hours, meaning 8.10 p.m. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was there a Colonel Lazic in the Bratunac Brigade at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Lazic arrived in the Bratunac Brigade, and I think he was in the Main Staff or in the Drina Corps. I know the man personally, but I'm not sure what his duty was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If I were to tell you that based on a document generated by the Prosecution office, that in the chart he is listed as being with the Drina Corps in the operations, the Drina Corps staff. Would that be consistent with your memory?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, according to this it would appear, would it not, sir, that it was not Colonel Blagojevic, the new commander of the Bratunac Brigade, who had just been installed that particular day, but rather a Colonel Lazic from the Drina Corps who had issued the order?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document confirms that. It says that Colonel Lazic ordered it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you -- can you recall having a conversation with Colonel Lazic ordering you, and do you know whether his order was transmitted to members of the Bratunac Brigade and then passed on to you?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this detail very well. My memory of it is really poor. I've thought about it all this time. Perhaps if I could see some of the combat reports. I know that we were targeted at our firing position then. Whether an enemy unit was infiltrated on that day and Bokser was killed, I remember that. I don't know if that could have been that day and that point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question now is: Why would Colonel Lazic be giving you an order, commander of the artillery unit? And why wouldn't that order not come from Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I think that's a mischaracterisation of what this said. It doesn't say that Colonel Lazic gave Mr. Gavric an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it says: "We opened fire on Srebrenica on Colonel Lazic's order."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: That's different than saying Colonel Lazic gave an order directly to Mr. Gavric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think Defence counsel is trying to clarify this issue through some questions to this witness. You may proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall getting an order directly from Colonel Lazic or getting an order from your new commander, Colonel Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but here it says at 1907 hours we opened fire on Srebrenica on orders from Colonel Lazic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go to the next document. And now I will be referring to what has been marked as P856. And I believe it's for identification, as was the other. This was shown to you as well. Now, from here, again this is the top part, it says: "25 May 1995," does it not? The very top part, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we go all the way to the bottom it says that it was sent or transmitted that same day at 2110 hours, which would have been, if we look at the previous document, one hour after you had submitted your report. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And if we look at the very first paragraph, it says: "Pursuant to Colonel Lazic's verbal order we fired ..." Does it not say that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, because this is an extraordinary -- an interim report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Okay. And if we go down to the second paragraph, the first line it says: "Brigade units are ordered to be in full combat readiness." Does it not say that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, searching back, rewinding the tape, as you put it, do you recall anything that would have placed the brigade on that particular day or that evening - because when we look at the normal daily report up until 4.00 there's nothing going on, or 4.30 - do you recall what might have happened between 4.30 when the daily combat report was sent off and 7.00 to have caused Colonel Lazic to issue an order, and also for the commander, the newly installed commander, to put the entire brigade units on full combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that on that day an enemy group was infiltrated behind our defence lines, and that a man whom we called Bokser in the 1st Battalion was killed, I think, on that day. And that's why I think Lazic issued this order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me show you what has been marked as P857 for identification purposes. Now, this dates 26 May 1995, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we go all the way down to the bottom, it looks like it was submitted at 1455. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we look at -- and this is a daily combat report, is it not, the title of it?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under number 2, it says: "The combat readiness of our unit is in accordance with the measures ordered by the superior command." Correct? Who would the superior command be?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that a handover was -- took place between Colonel Blagojevic and the command of the Drina Corps, and that Blagojevic in this period did not take over command over us until he had made a tour of the units and seen what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. It says under number 3: "Situation in the territory of the brigade's area of responsibility is normal." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that would -- so it would appear, at least in looking at paragraph number 3, that the situation is calmed down somewhat from the previous day as a result of having the units in full combat readiness, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I don't have a B/C/S version, but let me share with you what will be marked as D133 for identification purposes. And it's a chapter from the report prepared, the Nijad report, prepared by the Dutch government with respect to the fall of Srebrenica. And if we could put the second page on the ELMO, it's page 2 of 7. It states here -- I'll read it slowly. "Much of the Bosnian Serb revenge followed the NATO bombing of Pale on the 25 and 26 May concentrated on Sarajevo, but the eastern enclaves were not spared. This also had repercussions on the situation around Srebrenica. On May 25, as immediate retaliation, a number of shells landed close to a school in Srebrenica. There were one dead and three wounded. The VRS also opened fire on the south-western part of the enclave." Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, before your question, if this is a new document, document P133?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, what's this document -- would you please tell us some foundations or background to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I pulled this off the Internet. It's part of the Nijad report, the report by the Dutch government, where they had lengthy investigations. They generated, I believe, it's an 8.000-page report on the fall of Srebrenica or on Srebrenica itself. And so it -- the Dutch version has been published in volumes. The English version is available on the Internet. And we have made references to this particular report when the DutchBat soldiers were being questioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it would appear from reading this that NATO on May 25 and 26, just as it had bombed Belgrade, buildings, bridges, diplomatic missions, here was bombing Pale on 25 and 26 May, 1995. And according to the report, that there might have been a -- or there was a retaliation. Does this now cause you to recollect why you might have been ordered by Colonel Lazic to fire the artillery, as you so indicate in your report?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall. I really can't recall that detail. I'm sure we fired. I know we were targeted that day from a tank and that we returned anti-armour fire. One of our artillery pieces was destroyed. Some of my men were injured, but I'm sorry, I really can't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to move on to another section, and that was with respect to the artillery, your unit, and the questioning by the Prosecution with respect to the shells that were landing on and about Srebrenica and Potocari. First of all, sir, do you know whether there were any other artillery units operating in that vicinity -- and when I'm talking about the vicinity, I'm talking about the general Srebrenica area concerning the attack on Srebrenica that started on 6th July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you recall in my testimony of yesterday, I said that all the units that were operational in that area had their own artillery fire support of their own forces. Each unit had brought its own artillery with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to show you what has been marked and entered through evidence as D42. And we have an English version, or we should. We can put this on the ELMO, if necessary. And if you could take a look at that. Take a look at it first. And for the sake of time, let me tell you that this report was generated by Mr. Pandurevic at the time when he was the commander of the Zvornik Brigade. This is an order. If you could look at it, look it through.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need to look any further, because you can see from this order that there was 122 Howitzer, which means it was the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But I want to go through it in detail, because there are other -- we might see some other things that might be of interest to the Prosecution in light of their questioning. Where it says "order," we do see a Howitzer platoon of 122, do we not, under 1(e), right? Under (d), we see armoured mechanised company. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is there anything else on this page that might be of interest? If not, let's go to the next page. At the very bottom we see a tank platoon, four tanks, four T-55 tanks at the very bottom under 2.4(a). You see that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then if we can go on to (b), armoured mechanised platoon, four armoured personnel carriers. The one right after that, do you see it?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now if we go to (c), we see an anti-aircraft gun, and we see a Praga with crew.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to this line of questioning. It didn't really arise out of cross-examination. It's not relevant as part of our cross-examination. I believe that the issue is not who fired the shelling -- the shells. The issue is what this witness saw. And I believe he testified to that in the cross-examination. So at this point, we're just going into an irrelevant sideline of -- in questioning in the re-examination. And I don't believe -- I believe it falls outside the scope of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's well within the scope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I also wondered the relevance of this line of questions, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, the relevance, in my opinion, is rather clear, Your Honour. During the cross, during the cross, they read -- or she read an accounting of how many shells, where they landed, and so on and so forth. One would give the impression that they all came from the Bratunac Brigade or came from this gentleman's unit. What I'm trying to demonstrate here is: You have other units operating, that they well know, that are using the same kind of equipment, if not more. That -- and a close look at this particular order, because we know that the attack on Srebrenica was led -- was spearheaded, might I say, by the Zvornik Brigade or the elements that were led by Mr. Pandurevic. And here I'm trying to demonstrate that all this hardware existed with other units, and those units might have been responsible for any shells and not the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I don't think there's any disputes on this issue. We heard evidence that there was many units circling the Srebrenica area with the heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if there's a concession, Your Honour, by the Prosecution that all those shells that they recounted had nothing to do with the Bratunac Brigade and didn't come from the Bratunac Brigade, then I have no need to go over this, but I don't hear a concession on their part here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We can't say that. We just say that there are many, many Serb units circling Srebrenica with heavy weapons, including the Bratunac Brigade. You can't say that all the ammunitions are not from the -- that particular brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I brought the gentleman here so he could testify as to what the Bratunac Brigade had. They then went into all these other irrelevant matters. I stood up. I objected. I'm told, it's cross, it's not relevant -- or it's cross, it's permitted. On re-direct, I'm only trying to point the other picture. But since the document is in and it appears the Trial Chamber has understood the point that I'm trying to convey, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about Mr. Pilipovic. Do you recall? You were asked some questions?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you -- is it not a fact that you mentioned his name when you gave a statement to the Prosecution back on 28 November 2001? Is that not in your statement, his name?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Pilipovic's name should be there, because he showed me the report, not the combat one but the war one, which he wrote at his own initiative, I assume, and sent out to someone, I assume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question is: Did you not mention him when you spoke to the Prosecutor, so it would not be a surprise to you who this man is and how to spell his name, since you mentioned him on the 28th of November, 2001?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I forgot his name. We parted a long time ago and ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, you were asked some questions about intercepts, what they meant, what you were aware of. Were you aware that the Prosecution during the Krstic trial relied on an intercept and later on appeal that intercept proved to be wrong and as a result the Appeals Chamber has corrected the Trial Chamber based on their interpretation of the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: This is completely irrelevant and outside of the scope of the cross-examination. I don't see how that refers to the intercepts that I referred to in the cross-examinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm driving the point home, Your Honour, if we're going to ask people about intercepts that they have no absolutely idea with, that they were not part of that conversation, then it's all fair game, and the fair game is that they relied on an intercept during the Krstic trial that proved to be a false interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think that's your position. And it is useless to ask this kind of question to this witness. How could this witness know whether there is a judgement -- Appeals Judgement from the Krstic court?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't whether he knows, just about how would he know about that intercept between Indic and whoever else was talking. That was my point. But it's not my opinion. The judgement was very clear as to the Appeals Chamber interpretation of that intercept and its value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: In that intercept, a particular person's name was mentioned, so that maybe corroborates with the testimony of this witness or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I have no further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's absolutely uncalled-for him to be mentioning any Appeals Judgements, and his version of them in front of any witnesses, let alone make an argument. If we want to exchange views of the Krstic judgement and what it found, I mean I would gladly do that in this case. And in the end, his client would be convicted. But it's obscene for him to be doing that in this context, in this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let's save the discussion of that judgement for a later stage, maybe at the closing arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Other than that, I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, do you have any re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Just a few questions which result from the cross-examination. Further cross-examination by Mr. Stojanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gavric, may we clarify certain points that have emerged from the cross-examination led my Ms. Issa. On page 46 of the transcript of the LiveNote today, line 22, you were asked who Major Pilipovic was. And your answer was as follows: "He was a man who wrote a lot, did a lot of writing. Now, what he actually did, what his job was, I don't know to this day." Now, on page 47, line 16, of today's LiveNote, you go on to state the following: "In my opinion, that whole time, he was the duty officer."

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you try and clear that up for us, please. Do you think he was the duty officer throughout those days, or did you draw the conclusion based on some concrete specific order of appointment as duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there was an order of appointment of any kind. I think Pilipovic, as he was not a well man, couldn't go into the field, on the ground. I don't know whether I was clear enough; I'll try to be clearer now in explaining this. I don't know what position he held or whether he held any appointment, but as I say, as we were all engaged in our own affairs in those days, he spent most time at the command at the headquarters. And he performed the duty of duty officer in the operations hall for that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that you're not quite sure that Major Pilipovic on the 17th of July, when you returned from your assignment, was actually the duty officer as the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came across him there. He was inside, but I don't know whether he was actually the duty officer, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it would be possible that he wasn't the duty officer on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure there is a piece of paper that would bear that out. I don't know. I really can't remember after so much time has gone by. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you help us out with this, please: Whose responsibility was it, the security of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of intelligence, the security of the brigade, and in this case, probably as it was an operation of the Drina Corps, the Main Staff, then it must have been those people from the security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose responsibility was it?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of intelligence security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, yes. May I -- may we just take things slowly, and as you know everything has to be translated, the questions and answers, and we speak the same language, you and I. Now my question again: Whose duty was it or responsibility to take on responsibility or sanctions against somebody who unlawfully behaves towards the security of prisoners or criminally?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, the chief of security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was certainly not the job of the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, quite certainly it was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who sent you on this assignment specifically? Who told you to go and search the terrain on the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it then your duty and responsibility to inform the person you were responsible to about the activities, about the task you had performed?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my commander on that day went to Zepa, as he did do, the duty officer remained. So the duty officer in this case, as I encountered him there, was Mr. Pilipovic. So when I told him everything, Pilipovic was in charge and it was his responsibility to call the security officer to tell him what needed to be done. And this wasn't my duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's just it. I have before we Exhibit -- Defence Exhibit D11. It's instructions to the work of commands and staffs, providing for the duties of the duty officer. So am I right in saying what you have just actually told us, that it is the duty of the duty officer to convey further on what you had told him?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it cannot be the responsibility of the commanding staff -- the commanding staff and the duty officer don't have the same duties, do they, and responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they don't. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just let me go back to a point again and check it out. Sanctions against anybody engaged in unlawful conduct towards prisoners or to take steps against these persons would come under the duties of the duty officer. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It wouldn't be the duty of the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Judge Vassylenko. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Gospodin Gavric, I have only one question. Were you aware of the killing operations which resulted in the murder of several thousand able-bodied Muslim men in the Srebrenica enclave in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Hvala. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, are there any documents to tender? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe the one document you had suggested that we tender, that would be D132, that's the Bratunac Brigade -- it shouldn't read "Report," it should read "Information," dated 4 July 1994. And I believe D131, which is the "Consumption of Materiel and Equipment Submitted to the Drina Corps Command." And there is 134, which is the: "Daily combat report of 26 May, 1995." And there's D133 -- at least that portion of the paragraph read to the gentleman with respect to the NATO bombings of Pale on 25 or 26 May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections? Ms. Issa?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: None, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I have no exhibits to tender, but I have been warned that on page 74, line 24, of the transcript the answer was recorded that the witness did not give. That is to say that through my question, to confirm, that the security organ was the person who was intended to take steps against such persons; whereas, it states "duty officer." So I just wanted to put that right, to correct that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you very much. Well, the document D131, D132, D133, and D134 are admitted into evidence. Are there any documents on the part of the Prosecution to tender at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would like to tender documents P855 and 856.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Those two documents are admitted into the evidence. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. The usher will show you out of the room. We wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the Court's indulgence, may I be allowed to express my gratitude to you for enabling me to come to this courtroom and to present the truth that I knew about and to facilitate the work of you, as the Judges. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may go now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, before we have the next witness, there's one matter I would like to draw to the attention of the parties. In the proceedings, in order to avoid any unnecessary disputes between the parties, I hope whenever the parties address each other, they should address their counterparts by names or by positions, rather than by something else. I understand there must be some courtroom differences, so that's why I want both parties to abide by this ruling. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do. He should be here someplace in the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Are there any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Issa?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I wonder if I may be excused for this portion of the testimony, given that I'm finished with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you're not doing the cross-examination for the next witness, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: No, I'm not; it's Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, please. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could please tell us what your name is and tell us your -- just tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Zoran Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us your last name letter by letter.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: K-o-v-a-c-e-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Kovacevic, where are you from?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I'm from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Bjelovac, a village 6 kilometres from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you please tell us a little bit about your educational background.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I went to primary school in Bjelovac, and then eight years of secondary school in Bratunac. And then secondary catering school in Sabac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us about your work experience.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: From 1970, I worked for two years in Budva, that's the Montenegrin coast, as a waiter. And then 16 months later, I went to the Yugoslav People's Army. When I returned to Bratunac, where I started working in a catering establishment called Podrinje, which is where I worked until the war, and I'm working there now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you did your military service, could you tell us what was that all about? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I went to the school for reserve officers during my military service. It's a three-month course, after which I went to my unit. And I was the komandir of the department for recoilless guns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, from the time you left the JNA, your military service, until the time I assume you were mobilised, were you a reservist?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what rank, if any, did you hold?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I was a non-commissioned officer, and I had the rank of 2nd lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And during that period of time, did you do any drills as part of your reserve military service?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Mostly every other year we would have drills, us officers and NCOs. These would last for seven days. And the following seven days, we would be working with the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when the war broke out, were you mobilised?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you mobilised?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What position did you hold, if any, when you --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I was the komandir of the 3rd Company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And now, in that company how many soldiers were there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I had about 100 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to which company -- or this company belonged to which other unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It belonged to -- well, first of all, within the Territorial Defence. And later on when the brigade was established, we were in the composition of the 2nd Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So -- now, when the brigade was formed and this company became part of the 2nd Battalion, did it remain the 3rd Company?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the men, everything remained the same, in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it still the 3rd Company, or was it renamed -- given another number?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It was still the 3rd Company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And were you still the komandir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was your komandant at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: At that time the commander of the battalion -- well, I can't remember his name exactly. But the deputy battalion commander was Zoran -- Lieutenant Zoran Jovanovic throughout. They would replace each other. Battalion commanders moved around, so I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you please tell us where the 3rd Company of the 2nd Battalion was situated when the brigade was formed.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We were situated in the area from Zuti Most towards Voljevica, that is to say under Caus hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Zuti Most is on the road, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how far from the road or from the yellow bridge, the Zuti Most, how far from this location was your company located?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: My unit linked up the area from Zuti Most along the river itself to the part towards Voljevica, some 3 to 3 and a half kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now, if we get to the Zuti Most and we're heading towards Potocari or Srebrenica, on which side of the road would you be located?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: On the left-hand side of the road, moving from Bratunac to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, did this position ever change?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: This position remained that until 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to focus your attention to the month of July 1995. Were you still with the Bratunac Brigade at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I was. However, I was the komandir of the 4th Company of that same battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you please tell us where the 4th Company was situated.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The 4th Company was situated from the bottom of Caus hill along Obadi and Zalazi, along that line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, some of us haven't been there, so if you could show us or just describe to us. If you are by the Zuti Most, by the bridge, how far from there does your line begin?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: From Zuti Most, looking towards Srebrenica, it would be on the left-hand side. It is the Caus elevation, and Caus is a hill, and I would say that's 1 and a half kilometres as the crow flies. And then we go further to the left, about 300 metres from Caus on the other side, down the other slope, and that's where my unit went towards Zalazi, about 3 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're over the hill on the other side?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would I be correct in stating that from where you were situated, where the 3rd Company was situated, you could not look down and see the Zuti Most or see Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't the 3rd, but the 4th. Yes, that's correct. You couldn't see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, how long had you been with the 4th Company?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I remained in the 4th Company practically until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And how many men did the 4th Company have when it was at its position?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The company numbered 60 or 65 soldiers, it depended. They came and went. On the average, it was about 62 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long of a territory did you cover? What was the distance of the company?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately 2 and a half or 3 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, for 2 and a half to 3 kilometres, 60 men or 65 men would be spread out covering that line of defence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We had only seven or eight trenches with four or five men in each. There were places where we held only the elevations, and there might have been 7 or 800 metres between the -- one point and another. In normal conditions you would need 100 to 120 men to hold that line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the means of communications available to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We had only telephone -- wire communication. We did have some radio equipment, but it wasn't working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a Motorola?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was -- did you have a command post, so to speak, that is, the 4th Company?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the village of Obadi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just for the record, where was the command post for the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Near the Bratunac/Srebrenica road, in the village of Borici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that be on the other side of the mountain?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with your means of communication, where were you able to communicate? With whom?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In every trench, we had field telephones, wire communications, and I was able to communicate with the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to communicate with the headquarters in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No. Only through the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you might have answered the question, but let me ask it anyway. Were you able to communicate with the 3rd Battalion forward command post that was in Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I had no communications with the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that true also during the period of time when Srebrenica was attacked?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you could tell us -- well, let me just say about that. July 11th, 1995, is used as a reference point as the day when Srebrenica fell. Now, looking back from July 11, it's fairly established that July 6 is when the campaign against Srebrenica began. So from the 6th to the 11th, could you please describe to us the activities of your company, the 4th Company, of the 2nd Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Nothing essential changed. I think three or four days before I received an order from the battalion that I should set aside four or five men to strengthen the lines of defence in the 3rd Battalion. Everything else remained the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You said that you: "Needed to set aside four or five men to strengthen the lines of defence in the 3rd Battalion." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The command probably considered that there might be a counterattack on the lines of the 3rd Battalion, and most probably for this reason they needed to strengthen those lines. For this reason, they asked me to send some men, and so we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, incidentally, who was your neighbor to your right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Looking towards Srebrenica, my neighbor was an independent detachment - or what should I call it - with 15 or 20 men. They held the elevation of Caus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about on the opposite side? Who was your neighbour there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: On the other side, from the Oblo hill, there was the 3rd Battalion. I don't know what unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us what military hardware you had available at that location.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: You mean artillery pieces?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We had only infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, during that period, did you come into contact with enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us where you were on July 11th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I was in my unit at the line of defence among the men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when it was that you learn that Srebrenica had fallen.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I think this was through conversations with the communications squad in the battalion command, and I think it was only in the afternoon or the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That would be the evening of the 11th, July 11th?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that particular afternoon or evening, do you recall whether you received any orders for your company?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: During the evening, I received orders from the battalion containing my tasks for the next day, that is the 12th, and what the unit was to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we talk about the 12th, would you please tell us: Where did you spend that evening?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In the command of the company, the unit, at Obadi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, from that location to where your house is located, what is the distance?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It's about 2 kilometres between the headquarters and my house. But because it's a slope, you need about an hour to walk there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is your house located in relation to Bratunac town?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: My house is about 700 metres in the direction of Bratunac from the battalion command, or about 1 kilometre and 200 metres from the centre of the town of Bratunac in the direction of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And to the best of your recollection, that day, the day that Srebrenica fell, you did not go home, but rather you stayed with your unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the -- the next day, the 12th, do you recall what you did, you and your company.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I acted on the orders we had received the previous evening. That is, after the units that had taken that part, I set out toward Potocari along a part of the woods, and so I came down to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First, could you please tell us who gave you those orders.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I received the orders from the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you spoke to -- did you receive them personally or did you receive them from one of your men who was in communication with the command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: By telephone from people in the battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether it was the battalion commander himself that you spoke with, or did you speak with someone else?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but the order came from the battalion commander. It was his command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you could be as clear as possible, to the best of your recollection what exactly were you ordered to do?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We were ordered, when the units taking that part passed by, to follow them, to go down the right-hand side. This was below our defence line. It was a wood that nobody was holding. So to go through the wood and comb it, to make sure there were no enemy units or men in there, that was a strict order and that was our task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, which unit are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about my company, the 4th Company. And the other units were those who were doing Srebrenica. They weren't mentioned by name, but mention was just made of the units that would pass by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I just want to be very clear on this. Was this unit -- were you to follow this unit or were you working in conjunction with this unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We were to follow after that unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to the best of your recollection, do you know where this unit came from? Was it from the Bratunac Brigade? The Zvornik Brigade? Some other part of the Drina Corps? Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: All I know is that it was not a unit from the Bratunac Brigade, but I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And just one last question before we break for the day. Did you have an opportunity to speak with the commander of that unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the komandirs of some of those units? No. I had no close contact with them. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, thank you very much. I apologise for starting so late. And in light of the time, we'll -- I guess --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, I'm afraid we have to keep you here in The Hague for another day. And as I did to other witnesses in this trial, please do not talk to anybody and please do not let anybody talk to you about your testimony. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. The hearing for today is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
